meta.question: 我们准备在大学一年级 C 语言课程中允许学生使用生成式 AI 编程助手。它到底会不会提高学习效果？应该怎样引入？

research_frame.question: 我们准备在大学一年级 C 语言课程中允许学生使用生成式 AI 编程助手。它到底会不会提高学习效果？应该怎样引入？
research_frame.success_condition: independent problem solving and code quality improve (or do not decline) while AI dependency risk stays controlled; evidence base supports a bounded pilot.

decision.decision_question: 大一 C 语言课程是否应该允许学生使用生成式 AI 编程助手？
decision.target_population: university first-year computer science students learning C programming for the first time
decision.target_context: 16-week lecture-lab course, 60 students, TA support, offline
supported_claims: AI coding assistants reliably increase task performance during training (completion speed, correctness) — E-001, E-006.
Unguarded generative AI access can harm independent problem solving when access is removed — E-004.
Guardrail design (hints instead of answers) substantially mitigates the negative learning effect — E-005.
Task performance gains do not automatically imply learning gains — E-004 vs E-006 (within-study contrast).
uncertain_claims: Whether AI coding assistants improve or preserve actual programming learning in university novices — no direct university-level study in reviewed set.
Whether one-week neutral retention (Kazemitabaar 2023) extends to a semester — E-003.
contradicted_claims: The claim 'AI tools always improve learning' is contradicted by E-004 (unguarded access, -17% independent exam).
decision.reason_for_disagreement: Disagreement comes from outcome separation (task vs learning), tool design (guarded vs unguarded), and population (K-12 vs university). Studies measuring task performance show positive effects; the only study measuring independent learning after removal of AI shows harm without guardrails.
decision.methodology_summary: Two RCTs (one small K-12, one large high-school math) plus one mixed-methods undergraduate writing study. No direct RCT in university programming courses. All strong on internal validity; directness to the target context is weak.

outcome_specific_findings.assignment_score: positive during practice, negative on closed-book exam (E-004, E-006)
outcome_specific_findings.ai_dependency: documented crutch behavior with unguarded tool (E-004, E-005)

decision.short_term_effect: Task performance reliably increases; learning effect null-to-negative without guardrails.
decision.long_term_effect: No evidence beyond one week; long-term learning effect unknown.
decision.transfer_effect: No full transfer evidence; manual code-modification not harmed in one small study (E-002).
decision.risk_effect: AI dependency and over-reliance risk is real and documented for unguarded usage (E-004).

applicability.suitable_for: pilot in first-year C course with guardrailed usage policy
applicability.not_suitable_for: unrestricted AI adoption without usage policy

what_can_be_claimed: AI coding assistants raise task performance for novices during training.
Unguarded access carries a real risk of hurting independent problem solving.
Guardrail design can mitigate that risk.
Direct evidence for university C programming learning is missing.
what_cannot_be_claimed: AI coding assistants improve (or even preserve) university students' programming learning.
Any claim about which students benefit, based on university samples.
missing_evidence: RCT of AI coding assistants in university programming courses with retention and no-AI transfer tests.
Studies varying AI usage policy within the same course.
Longitudinal data on AI dependency beyond one course.
decision.decision_rationale: Positive task-performance evidence plus documented unguarded-access risk and missing university-level learning evidence → bounded, guardrailed pilot with evaluation, not full adoption.
exceeds_evidence_boundary: 'AI 编程助手提高学习效果' — exceeds: direct learning-effect evidence is missing.
'AI 对所有人有效' — exceeds: population and subject mismatch.

claims.claim: AI coding assistants significantly increase task completion speed and completion rate during training.
Access to AI code generation did not decrease performance on manual code-modification tasks.
One week after training, retention differences between Codex and baseline groups did not reach statistical significance.
Students with unguarded GPT-4 access performed 17% worse on the independent exam than the control group, despite higher practice performance.
Guardrail design of the AI tutor (hints instead of answers, teacher-informed prompts) largely eliminated the negative learning effect.
Access to GPT-4 during practice improves task performance (48% for GPT Base, 127% for GPT Tutor) — but this task performance does not transfer to independent exam performance.
ChatGPT as a formative feedback tool produced a significant positive impact on students' academic writing skills with positive student perceptions.

evidence.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
evidence.subject: mathematics
evidence.population: nearly a thousand high school math students in Turkey
evidence.outcome_measure: exam without access to AI resources after practice phase
evidence.claim: Students with unguarded GPT-4 access performed 17% worse on the independent exam than the control group, despite higher practice performance.
evidence.method: large-scale randomized controlled trial, practice phase then closed-book exam

evidence.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
evidence.subject: mathematics
evidence.population: nearly a thousand high school math students in Turkey
evidence.outcome_measure: exam without access to AI resources after practice phase
evidence.claim: Guardrail design of the AI tutor (hints instead of answers, teacher-informed prompts) largely eliminated the negative learning effect.
evidence.effect: negative effect essentially eradicated, no positive effect observed

evidence.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
evidence.subject: mathematics
evidence.population: nearly a thousand high school math students in Turkey
evidence.outcome_measure: practice problem performance during study sessions
evidence.claim: Access to GPT-4 during practice improves task performance (48% for GPT Base, 127% for GPT Tutor) — but this task performance does not transfer to independent exam performance.

evidence.title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students' academic writing skills
evidence.subject: academic_writing_esl
evidence.population: undergraduate ESL students at an Indian university

evidence.effect: significant positive impact on writing skills
evidence.method: mixed methods intervention study, pre/post/delayed tests and focus groups

control_group.note: All three studies include a no-AI control group.

randomization.note: Kazemitabaar 2023 and Bastani 2025 use randomized assignment.

pre_test.note: Kazemitabaar 2023 has a pre-study evaluation; Bastani 2025 measures baseline covariates.

post_test.note: Immediate post-tests present in all studies.

retention_test.note: Kazemitabaar 2023 has 1-week retention; Bastani 2025 has no delayed test; Marzuki 2024 has delayed test.

transfer_test.note: Kazemitabaar 2023 code-modification task is transfer-adjacent; no full no-AI transfer task.

sample_bias.note: Bastani 2025 nearly 1000 students; Kazemitabaar 2023 small (69) young sample.

measurement_validity.note: Practice/task performance is not equated to learning; independent exams present in Bastani 2025 only.

confounders.note: Prior programming competency interacts with AI benefit in Kazemitabaar 2023.

instructor_effect.note: Kazemitabaar 2023 is self-paced; classroom studies may carry instructor effects.

novelty_effect.note: Short interventions likely inflate engagement; none of the studies controlled for novelty.

tool_version_effect.note: Single tool versions studied; rapid tool change limits durability.

ai_usage_policy.note: Bastani 2025 explicitly contrasts unguarded vs guardrailed usage policies.

dropout.note: Marzuki 2024 reports attrition; others not detailed.

task_vs_learning_guard.note: Bastani 2025 demonstrates the danger of equating the two: +48-127% practice performance coexisted with -17% independent exam performance.

limitations: No randomized study of AI coding assistants in university C programming courses was found in the reviewed set.
Task performance gains are consistently large, learning-effect estimates are null-to-negative and subject-mismatched.
Retention evidence exists for only one week (Kazemitabaar 2023).
suggestions: Treat all learning-effect conclusions as requiring direct university-level studies.
Design the pilot with guardrails modeled on Bastani 2025's GPT Tutor (hints, not answers).
Include a no-AI transfer task in the evaluation plan.

conflicts.reason_for_disagreement: Disagreement comes from outcome separation (task vs learning), tool design (guarded vs unguarded), and population (K-12 vs university). Studies measuring task performance show positive effects; the only study measuring independent learning after removal of AI shows harm without guardrails.

applicability.suitable_for: pilot in first-year C course with guardrailed usage policy
applicability.not_suitable_for: unrestricted AI adoption without usage policy

intervention.target_learners: university first-year C programming students (60-student lecture-lab class)
learning_goals: independently write and debug small C programs without AI
understand core concepts: variables, conditionals, loops, arrays, pointers
use AI tools critically as explanation and debugging aids, not answer machines

phase_1.name: Phase 1 — Independent Foundation
activities: first 2 weeks of assignments completed without any AI code generation
phase_1.ai_usage_rule: full code generation forbidden; AI allowed only for conceptual explanations

phase_2.name: Phase 2 — Explain, Don't Solve
activities: weeks 3-4: AI allowed to explain errors, concepts and debugging approaches
phase_2.ai_usage_rule: AI may explain but must not produce full solutions

phase_3.name: Phase 3 — Structured Collaboration
activities: weeks 5-7: AI allowed to generate partial code; students must explain every AI-generated block in their own words
phase_3.ai_usage_rule: partial code generation allowed; mandatory written explanation of key logic; submission requires reasoning trace
phase_3.outcome_check: weekly lab completion and code-quality rubric

phase_4.name: Phase 4 — Transfer Check
activities: week 8: new programming task completed in a no-AI environment
phase_4.ai_usage_rule: no AI access during transfer assessment
phase_4.outcome_check: transfer test score, independent problem solving

intervention.ai_usage_policy: AI usage is allowed in three explicitly graded modes (explain / collaborate / no-AI-transfer). Copying unexamined AI output is an academic integrity violation and is assessed via the reasoning-trace requirement.
intervention.teacher_role: design guardrailed prompts and rubrics; monitor usage logs; hold weekly reflection debriefs
intervention.student_role: complete assignments in the allowed mode; submit reasoning traces; reflect on when AI helped vs. when it masked understanding
intervention.reflection_requirement: students must explain key AI-generated logic in their own words; one written reflection per phase
intervention.assessment: no-AI baseline quiz, mid-pilot quiz, no-AI transfer task, code-quality rubric, AI-usage self-report
risk_control: guardrailed usage policy modeled on Bastani 2025 GPT Tutor (hints, not answers)
no-AI transfer assessment prevents grade inflation from task-performance gains
usage logs reviewed weekly to detect crutch behavior
stop_conditions: transfer-test scores drop significantly below baseline cohort expectations
widespread integrity violations in reasoning traces
AI dependency signals exceed threshold in risk metrics

evaluation.research_question: In a first-year C programming course, does a guardrailed AI coding assistant (explain-only → structured collaboration) improve independent problem solving without increasing AI dependency, compared to no-AI instruction?

groups.treatment: two lab sections using the 4-phase guardrailed AI policy
groups.comparison: two matched lab sections without AI access (same instructor and materials)

evaluation.baseline: week-1 no-AI programming quiz (independent problem solving, completion time)
evaluation.post_test: week-8 no-AI programming quiz (independent problem solving, code quality)
evaluation.retention_test: final exam (week 16) — delayed measure 8 weeks after pilot
evaluation.transfer_test: week-8 novel programming task in a strictly no-AI environment
process_metrics: AI usage logs: prompts submitted, copied blocks, reasoning traces
risk_metrics: AI dependency index (usage without understanding, from reasoning-trace quality)
false confidence (post-quiz confidence vs actual score)
evaluation.analysis_plan: pre-registered comparison of treatment vs comparison sections on baseline-adjusted learning metrics (ANCOVA); task-performance metrics reported separately from learning metrics; subgroup analysis by prior programming competency; stop-condition monitoring at weeks 3, 5, 7.
evaluation.success_threshold: treatment group shows non-inferior independent problem solving (delta within 5%) AND superior or equal retention AND AI dependency index below threshold; if independent problem solving declines >10%, the pilot is judged unsuccessful regardless of task-performance gains.
stop_conditions: AI dependency index exceeding pre-set threshold for two consecutive weeks
